passage:
Wednesday, hostel room, 11 pm
Economics lecture today: slides in one tab, class chat in another, a shopping site in a third, plus my notes in a doc. I felt like a pilot with all the screens. Indu, sitting next to me, whispered, "Look at this boy, running an airport."
Tonight I opened my notes to revise. Half the sentences stop in the middle. One line just says "demand curve, ask later???" I can't remember a single example the professor gave, even though I was sitting right there. Payal's handwritten notes have three examples and a diagram.
I think every time I flicked to the chat, I lost the thread and caught up only halfway. It felt efficient. It wasn't.
Tomorrow: only the notes open, chat closed, phone in my bag. Let's see.
Harshad

qa.a: One line just says "demand curve, ask later???"

qa.q: What choice does Harshad make for tomorrow, and how can he tell if it works?
qa.a: Only the notes open, chat closed, phone in the bag; comparing tomorrow's notes with today's broken sentences will show whether it helps.

qa.q: What do Payal's handwritten notes suggest about how the lecture went for Payal?
qa.a: With three examples and a diagram, Payal seems to have followed the professor steadily, which shows the lecture could be followed with full attention.

grounding: It shows a male student with many tabs open during a lecture who feels efficient but ends up with broken notes and little memory.

passage:
At the district college, Chetan was the only one in his row with a laptop, a gift from his uncle. During the botany lecture he kept his notes file open, and beside it a cricket score page and a chat with his friends from the bus. He felt sharp, switching every minute.
Leela, sitting behind him with a thin spiral notebook, wrote steadily.
That evening, on the crowded bus home, they revised for Friday's test. Leela read out the parts of the flower from her notebook. Chetan scrolled through his file: fragments, a missing diagram, "sepal?? petal??"
"You were typing the whole hour," Leela said.
"Typing the wrong things," Chetan admitted. The next day he kept the score page closed and sat beside her.

qa.a: Leela read out the parts of the flower from her notebook.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel sharp while switching every minute?

qa.q: What did Chetan change the next day, and why might it help?
qa.a: He kept the score page closed and sat beside Leela, cutting the switches so the lecture could get his attention.

qa.q: How might Leela see the difference between her notebook and Chetan's laptop?
qa.a: Leela may see that the plain notebook kept her with the lecture, while the laptop's extra pages pulled Chetan away despite being the fancier tool.

passage: In the computer lab at the engineering college in Warangal, Ganga ma'am was explaining loops on the big screen. passage: Himani, you asked why I switched to paper notes this semester. Honestly, it's because of one lecture. I'm Lalit. In first year I'd sit in economics with my laptop open: lecture slides in one tab, the class chat in another, a cricket score, sometimes a shopping site. I felt like a machine, following everything at once. Then, before the mid-term, I opened my notes for the lecture on inflation. Half-sentences. 'Demand pull... see slide?' A grocery list in the middle. I couldn't remember a single example the professor gave, though I'd sat in the front row. So now the laptop stays in my bag. Paper, one pen, phone face down. It feels slower in class. But in the exam I actually remembered the examples, and I didn't have to relearn a whole unit.

passage:
In a crowded seminar room in Mumbai, Sumit sat at the back with his laptop: slides in one window, a group chat in another, a video paused in a third. He felt sharp and busy.

The lecturer, Dr Madhuri, stopped mid-sentence. "Sumit, what did I just say about the second method?"

Sumit blinked. He had heard her voice the whole time. "The... second method is... better?"

A few people laughed. His ears burned.

After class, he checked his notes. There were bits of three lectures mixed up, and one line that said "ask about lunch."

The next week, he closed everything but the slides and a blank page. For the first time in weeks, he could explain the lecture to his roommate.

qa.q: What did Dr Madhuri ask Sumit about?
qa.a: What she just said about the second method.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when his ears burned?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and caught out, realising he'd heard her voice but taken in nothing.

qa.q: What did Sumit change the next week, and why did it help?
qa.a: He closed everything but the slides and a blank page, so his attention stayed with the lecture.

qa.q: How might Dr Madhuri see students like Sumit with many windows open?
qa.a: She might feel frustrated or concerned that they believe they are listening when they aren't.

grounding: A student with slides, chat and video open thinks he can follow all, but his notes and memory suffer.

passage:
In my first year of engineering, I was proud of my lecture set-up. I'm Siddharth, and I had it all: slides in one tab, notes in another, the class chat in a third and sports scores in a fourth. I felt like I was in a control room.
Then the mid-semester exam came. I opened my notes for the electronics lecture and found half-sentences. "Transistor gain is... (see slide?)" Whole diagrams missing. I remembered the cricket score from that day perfectly.
My friend Shankar, who wrote notes by hand with his laptop shut, lent me his. They were clear, complete, even funny in places.
I realised I hadn't been following four things. I'd been jumping between them so fast that none got my attention for more than a few seconds.
Now I keep one tab open in class: the slides. Everything else waits for the break. My notes are boring. They're also actually notes.

qa.q: How many tabs did Siddharth have open in lectures?
qa.a: Four tabs: slides, notes, the class chat and sports scores.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth feel proud of the lecture set-up?
qa.a: Siddharth felt efficient and in control, like being in a control room, without noticing that attention was jumping every few seconds.

qa.q: What does Siddharth do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Keeps one tab, the slides, open in class and leaves everything else for the break, so attention stays on the lecture.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt lending the notes?
qa.a: Shankar was probably happy to help, and maybe a little amused that the control room produced half-sentences.

grounding: Shows a student who expected to follow tabs, chat and lecture at once, until the notes and exam showed the cost of switching.

passage:
Professor's note, second-year economics, week 8. Written by Darshan.
Tanvir sits in the third row with a laptop open. From the front I can see him switching every few seconds: my slides, a chat window, a shopping site, back to my slides. He types quickly and looks busy. He probably thinks he is following everything.
In today's quiz, Tanvir could not explain the demand curve we had discussed for twenty minutes. He looked genuinely confused, as if hearing it for the first time.
I spoke to him after class. I didn't scold. I asked him to try one experiment: next lecture, laptop closed, pen and paper only. Then compare.
He agreed, a little reluctantly.
What I did next: I've started a two-minute "screens down" summary at the end of each lecture for the whole class, where everyone writes the main point in their own words.

qa.q: How long had the class discussed the demand curve?
qa.a: The class had discussed the demand curve for twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir probably think he was following everything?
qa.a: Tanvir felt busy and efficient, typing quickly and switching fast, which felt like keeping up.

qa.q: What experiment did Darshan suggest, and why?
qa.a: Laptop closed and pen and paper only for one lecture, then compare, to show how switching was hurting understanding.

qa.q: How did Darshan see Tanvir in the quiz?
qa.a: Darshan saw a student who looked genuinely confused, as if hearing it for the first time, and chose to help rather than scold.

grounding: Shows, in a professor's note, a student switching between lecture, chat and shopping who thinks he is following but remembers little.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Yamini asked me today what the professor said about the case study deadline. I had been in the same lecture, front row, laptop open. I had no idea.
I remember what I did in that lecture: replied to the hostel group, checked a job site, started an email, glanced at the slides. It felt so efficient. I was doing four things!
But I can't remember a single thing the professor said. Yamini, who only had a notebook, remembered the deadline, the three examples and a joke about bananas.
I think I was doing four things badly instead of one thing well. Switching felt like speed, but it wasn't.
Tomorrow: laptop in the bag, notebook out. If I need to reply to something, I'll do it in the break.
Vishal
